description:
We are a team from Women in Science (WIS), an initiative that promotes the participation, education, and leadership of girls and women in STEM. We are driven by scientific curiosity, creativity, and a shared passion for exploring how science and technology can help us better understand our universe.
For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we will be working on “Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.”
summary: Órbita Arcade is a free browser game portal where kids aged 9 to 14 learn how NASA's abandoned machines on the Moon and Mars worked, by doing what those machines did. Eighteen short games, 54 levels and 46 science concepts put real hardware in your hands: grind a rock with Opportunity's RAT before reading its chemistry, get Spirit stuck in soft sand, time the laser echo to a mirror Apollo 15 left on the Moon, land Pathfinder through thin Martian air. There are no quizzes: the science is the rule of the game, so the only way to win is to understand it. Every important decision is recorded as a concept learned or missed, and a private teacher dashboard shows what each student understood. Every fact links to a NASA source, with 50 sources registered. It answers the challenge by turning silent artifacts into playable stories for school-age explorers, works on computers and phones, and supports reduced motion and screen readers. Some machines stopped moving, but they can still spark questions.
details:
ORBITA ARCADE: ECHOES FROM OTHER WORLDS

Team WISe · Challenge: Abandoned but not Forgotten · NASA Space Apps 2026

Live on Vercel: https://wise-orbita-arcade.vercel.app

Source code: https://github.com/FabiCasC/WISe---Frontend

1. OUR ANSWER TO THE CHALLENGE

The challenge says school-age space fans “often hear only about active, ongoing missions”, while hardware left on the Moon and Mars holds “rich, untold histories”, and it invites projects that bring “silent or active artifacts” back to life.

Órbita Arcade turns that hardware into short games for kids aged 9 to 14. We use the challenge’s own range of artifacts:

Machines that went silent: Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, Sojourner and Pathfinder, and Ingenuity, whose mission ended in 2024.

Hardware left behind on purpose or after use: the Apollo descent stages, the Lunar Roving Vehicles and the science packages left on the Moon.

Instruments still working today: the Apollo 15 laser retroreflector.

Infrastructure that lets us find and hear these machines: the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), which photographs the abandoned Apollo sites from orbit, and NASA’s Deep Space Network (DSN), the antennas that keep contact with distant probes. These two are active; we do not call them abandoned.

A spacecraft that ended its life on purpose: DART, which hit the moonlet Dimorphos.

2. WHAT DOES IT DO AND HOW DOES IT WORK?

What it does: Órbita Arcade is a free browser portal with 18 short games, 54 levels and 46 science concepts. Each game is built around one real machine and one real constraint it faced, such as a battery that could not be recharged, a 10 to 15 minute radio delay, or air less than 1% as dense as Earth’s. The player solves a challenge inspired by that decision, and the only way to succeed is to apply the science.

How it works:

Student (phone or computer, nickname only)

→ Portal (React, TypeScript, Vite): accounts, progress and medals saved in the browser

→ Game (Phaser 3 or Canvas 2D): returns a score and a list of decisions, each marked as a concept learned or missed

→ Teacher dashboard: concepts and medals per student, the concept the class finds hardest, and a suggested 2-minute classroom discussion.

The student picks a machine and plays Level 0, a guided practice where nothing counts.

They play three levels, each built on one real decision.

Every key decision is saved as a concept learned or missed.

The teacher opens the class panel and reads what each student understood.

Where the data lives today: progress, classes and the teacher dashboard are stored in the browser (local storage). A teacher sees a class only on the device and browser where it was created. Sharing a class across devices needs server-side infrastructure that we have not built yet. We chose this for the prototype so there is no account data on a server, and because there was no time to build and secure one in the hackathon.

The 18 machines:

Two Signals from the Moon: Apollo 15 retroreflector and seismometer.

Eagle Liftoff: Apollo 11 lunar module.

Artemis Landing: lunar landers.

Moon Buggy Run: Lunar Roving Vehicles.

Seen from Orbit: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter imagery of Apollo sites.

Lunar Express: Apollo samples and left-behind experiments.

NASA Number Mission: numbers behind the retroreflector.

Opportunity Echoes: Opportunity rover.

Spirit’s Last Route: Spirit rover.

Storm over Meridiani: Opportunity and the 2018 dust storm.

Gusev Maze: Spirit’s solar panels.

Sun and Shade: solar and nuclear power on Mars rovers.

Pathfinder Bounce: Mars Pathfinder.

Sojourner’s Plan: Sojourner rover.

Phoenix Ice Dig: Phoenix lander.

Ingenuity: Fly in Thin Air: Ingenuity helicopter.

Keep the Link: Deep Space Network.

DART Impact: DART spacecraft.

3. WHAT MAKES OUR LEARNING METHOD DIFFERENT

Students learn by applying a scientific principle to solve a challenge inspired by a decision real mission teams faced. They do not read a fact and then answer a question about it. For example, in Spirit’s Last Route the student decides whether to cross soft sand, as the real rover did before it got stuck; in Pathfinder Bounce they time the parachute, the rockets and the airbags in thin air.

This changes what we can measure. A quiz records whether a student remembers an answer. Our games record whether the student made a sound decision under the machine’s real constraint, and the teacher sees that as a concept learned or missed.

How the 46 concepts were chosen: for each machine, the team picked claims that its NASA source supports and that can become a decision (for example, “dust devils sometimes cleaned Spirit’s panels”). Each claim became one concept with an identifier that the game reports and the teacher panel counts. Thirteen games teach three concepts (one per level), two games teach two, and three games teach one. The team identified the concepts from NASA sources; they have not yet been reviewed by teachers or education researchers.

4. WHAT RESEARCH SUPPORTS OUR DESIGN, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT

Wouters, P., van Nimwegen, C., van Oostendorp, H., & van der Spek, E. D. (2013). A meta-analysis of the cognitive and motivational effects of serious games. Journal of Educational Psychology, 105(2), 249-265. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031311

It reports that serious games improve learning and retention over conventional instruction, with larger effects when games are combined with other instruction, played over several sessions and played in groups. Our decisions: a teacher dashboard and classroom discussion pair every game with other instruction, and each machine has three levels.

Sailer, M., & Homner, L. (2020). The gamification of learning: a meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 77-112. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09498-w

It reports small to moderate positive effects of gamification on cognitive, motivational and behavioral outcomes. Our decision: we use game mechanics to carry the science itself instead of adding points on top of a quiz.

These studies support the approach in general. They do not show that our portal works; we have not tested it with students.

5. THE PROBLEM IN CONTEXT: THREE COMPLEMENTARY SOURCES

These sources come from different populations, years and measures. We do not compare them with each other; each one shows one side of the problem.

TIMSS 2019 (international student survey) shows how attitudes change with age: 52% of fourth graders “very much like” learning science, against 35% of eighth graders. It points to a drop of interest in the 9 to 14 range we designed for. https://timssandpirls.bc.edu/timss2019/international-results/students-like-learning-mathematics-and-science/index.html

PISA 2022 (OECD, 15-year-olds, Peru) shows science proficiency in one country: 47% reached Level 2 or higher, against 76% on average in OECD countries, and 1% were top performers, against 7%. It shows why science learning needs more entry points, in the country where our team works. https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/pisa-2022-results-volume-i-and-ii-country-notes_ed6fbcc5-en/peru_3e71791c-en.html

Joan Ganz Cooney Center teacher survey, 2014 (United States, 694 K-8 teachers) shows how teachers use games: 74% use digital games, but 42% found them helpful for teaching science, against 71% for math. It is old and from another country, so we use it only to show that teachers rate science games lower. https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/digital-learning-games-used-by-majority-of-teachers-survey-finds/2014/10

None of these shows that our portal improves learning.

6. STATUS: AVAILABLE, IN DEVELOPMENT, ROADMAP

Available now (deployed):

18 playable games, 54 levels, 46 concepts.

Level 0 for each game: a three-screen guide (what you will learn, how to play, what each part of the screen means) and a practice mode.

Nickname-only accounts, a profile with rank and medals (15 for students, 17 for teachers), class codes and a teacher dashboard, all stored in the browser.

50 registered NASA sources with link and access date, and a plain note in each game on what the game simplifies or invents.

More than 600 automated tests; browser checks of every game.

In development (redesign in a pull request, not yet in the deployed version):

Technical terms underlined and explained in one line when tapped.

A short recap at the end of each level, built from what the player did.

A new Opportunity Echoes in which tiles act on a rock with three spots, and a new NASA Number Mission, “Find the Beacon”, that replaces its guessing mechanic.

A hook per game: short rounds, visible tension, three stars and a replay that explains what happened.

Roadmap (not started):

A classroom pilot with real students and teachers.

Server-side infrastructure to share classes across devices.

A block-based Studio so students can build their own game from a machine, a rule, a goal and a sourced fact.

Games for Viking, InSight, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer and Kepler.

7. TOOLS AND AI-ASSISTED DEVELOPMENT

Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite.

Games: Phaser 3 (Opportunity and Spirit) and Canvas 2D with shared helpers.

Quality: Vitest, with tests that every level is winnable, that the required science is really required, and that random play almost never wins; Playwright for browser checks.

Delivery: GitHub with automatic checks on every pull request; Vercel hosting that publishes on merge.

Data: 50 NASA sources registered with link and access date; NASA/JPL photographs with credit.

Typefaces: Orbitron, Nunito, IBM Plex Mono and Space Grotesk (open licences).

AI-assisted development: Claude Code (Anthropic) helped write and review code, tests and documentation, and drafted some text. The team chose the idea, the machines, the science and the sources, and reviewed and tested the result. No NASA logo or identifier was generated or altered.

8. WHAT IS CREATIVE ABOUT IT

“Abandoned” becomes “unfinished”: each machine is a character whose last mission the player completes.

The science is the mechanic: a broken wheel digs up bright soil, a dust devil cleans a panel, a lower orbit catches the ship ahead.

Two audiences: kids get a game, teachers get evidence of understanding.

Openness about gameplay simplifications: each game states what it invents, and we corrected our own scientific errors during an audit against the sources.

9. DESIGN CRITERIA AND LIMITS

Age: short games, plain words and a Level 0 for every game.

Controls: keyboard, mouse and touch.

Accessibility, what is implemented: a reduced-motion setting, labels and announcements for screen readers, readable text on phones. What has been tested: we run automated browser checks. What has not been tested: use with real screen readers or by students with disabilities, and no accessibility standard has been audited, so we do not claim compliance with one.

Privacy: accounts need only a nickname; no real names or emails; data stays in the browser.

Accuracy: every fact is linked to a NASA source; in the audit we fixed a game that said something false about a nuclear rover and a game that could be won by random play.

Weight: the portal’s initial load is about 135 KB gzipped.

Known limits: no tests with children or teachers yet; no server; the Studio editor is a placeholder; six NASA machines have no game.

10. MISSION LOG: ONE ENTRY PER MACHINE

Each entry has four parts: historical context, what the player does, expected learning, and what the game simplifies or invents.

THE MOON

Log 01 · Two Signals from the Moon · Apollo 15 retroreflector and seismometer

Historical context: Apollo 15 landed on 30 July 1971. It left a laser retroreflector with 300 corner cubes that needs no power and is still used today, and a science station that ran until 30 September 1977. A laser pulse takes about 2.5 seconds to go to the Moon and back; the Moon is about 384,400 km away on average.

What the player does: times the echo of a laser and turns it into a distance, then places seismometer stations until three circles cross at the spot of a moonquake.

Expected learning: light can measure distance because it goes and returns; one station is not enough to locate a quake; with too few stations, a scientist says the data is not enough.

Simplified or invented: the stopwatch, the stations and the quake positions.

Log 02 · Eagle Liftoff · Apollo 11 lunar module

Historical context: Eagle’s ascent engine fired for 435 seconds into an 11 by 55 mile orbit, lower than Columbia’s. Since a lower circular orbit is faster, Eagle caught up and docked about three and a half hours later. The descent stage stayed on the Moon and is still at Tranquility Base.

What the player does: lifts off at the right moment, drops to a lower orbit to catch Columbia, then climbs back to dock.

Expected learning: the launch window, and why catching a spacecraft ahead of you means moving to a lower, faster orbit first.

Simplified or invented: time is sped up and each burn jumps straight to the next circular orbit, while a real change takes two burns.

Log 03 · Artemis Landing · lunar landers

Historical context: the Moon has no atmosphere, so a parachute cannot slow a lander and landings are flown mainly on engine thrust. Gravity is 1.62 m/s², a sixth of Earth’s, but it never stops pulling, so hovering burns fuel without lowering the lander. On Apollo 11 the low-fuel warning came on while Armstrong was still looking for smooth ground.

What the player does: lands softly and level using one engine and side thrusters.

Expected learning: with no air to brake against, the engine does the slowing; fuel is time in disguise; low gravity is still gravity.

Simplified or invented: a real descent takes about twelve minutes and is mostly flown by computer; the game is one short 2D fall.

Log 04 · Moon Buggy Run · Lunar Roving Vehicles

Historical context: three rovers were driven on Apollo 15, 16 and 17 and all three were left on the Moon. Each had two 36-volt batteries that could not be recharged and a navigation computer that kept track of the way back. The farthest drives were 5.0, 4.5 and 7.6 km.

What the player does: collects samples and returns before the battery runs out; later, never leaves the circle from which the crew could walk back.

Expected learning: with a battery that cannot be recharged, a route is planned around the way home.

Simplified or invented: a small, sped-up map, the battery counted in metres, and the size of the walk-back circle.

Log 05 · Seen from Orbit · Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (still active)

Historical context: since 2009 LRO has photographed the Apollo sites, showing descent stages, experiments and astronauts’ footpaths. At Apollo 14 a worn path joins the lander to the experiments about 180 m away. With the Sun 28 degrees higher over Apollo 11, shadows shrank and faint brightness differences stood out.

What the player does: chooses the Sun angle that reveals the hardware, follows a footpath and compares two photos.

Expected learning: a low Sun shows height through long shadows, a high Sun shows brightness differences, and comparing photos requires comparable light.

Simplified or invented: the pictures are drawn by the game, not real LRO images; shadow length follows the real rule, height divided by the tangent of the Sun angle.

Log 06 · Lunar Express · Apollo samples and left-behind experiments

Historical context: the Moon has bright highlands, older crust, and dark maria, seas of lava that cooled between 4.2 and 1.2 billion years ago. Apollo crews brought back rocks from both and left science packages on purpose; the seismometers sent data until 1977.

What the player does: carries the right kind of rock in a growing line, and sets science packages down away from the lunar module.

Expected learning: the Moon’s history can be read from its rocks, and some hardware was left behind on purpose to keep doing science.

Simplified or invented: the line of samples, the oxygen time and the distance rule for packages. Real rocks come in many shades.

Log 07 · NASA Number Mission · the retroreflector’s numbers

Historical context: the same Apollo 15 retroreflector as Log 01, with 300 corner cubes, no power needed and still in use. A laser pulse takes about 2.5 seconds to travel to the Moon and back, over about 384,400 km on average.

What the player does: narrows down a measured number by halving the range, and sees that every measurement has a margin of error.

Expected learning: halving the range finds a number in few tries; distance, the speed of light and echo time are linked.

Simplified or invented: the search rules, the number of attempts and the points.

MARS

Log 08 · Opportunity Echoes · Opportunity rover

Historical context: Opportunity landed in Meridiani Planum on 25 January 2004 and sent its last signal on 10 June 2018, during a global dust storm. NASA declared the mission complete on 13 February 2019. It found hematite-rich concretions and gypsum veins, minerals typically formed in the presence of liquid water, and it did not find evidence of life.

What the player does: matches the rover’s tools on a tile board to photograph, grind and analyze a rock, using the rover’s own order of work. In the version in development, the tiles act on a rock with three spots and the player ends by sending a report with several clues.

Expected learning: look before you touch, grind before you read, and one clue is not enough to conclude.

Simplified or invented: the tile board and the readings; real rovers did not match tiles.

Log 09 · Spirit’s Last Route · Spirit rover

Historical context: in May 2009 Spirit got stuck in soft sand near Home Plate and never drove again. Earlier, a broken front wheel dragged across the ground and dug up bright soil rich in silica, a clue to hot water. In winter Spirit parked on slopes that face the low Sun.

What the player does: crosses soft sand, uncovers bright soil with a broken wheel and parks on the slope that gives the most power.

Expected learning: soft sand drains power and can trap a rover; bright silica suggests hot water; tilting panels toward the winter Sun produces more power.

Simplified or invented: rovers do not jump; the jumping and the timing are gameplay simplifications.

Log 10 · Storm over Meridiani · Opportunity and the 2018 dust storm

Historical context: Opportunity ran on solar panels. In June 2018 a planet-wide dust storm darkened the sky; the dust opacity, called tau, climbed to about 10.8, almost no sunlight got through, and its last signal came on 10 June.

What the player does: keeps driving while the sky darkens and energy drains; the last level uses the real storm.

Expected learning: less sunlight means less power, and the more dust in the air, the less a solar rover can charge.

Simplified or invented: the rover moved a few centimetres per second and never ran or jumped; those are gameplay simplifications to let the player feel the light fading.

Log 11 · Gusev Maze · Spirit’s solar panels

Historical context: in Gusev crater dust settled on Spirit’s solar panels and cut its power. Passing dust devils sometimes blew the dust away and its power jumped back up; the team called these cleaning events.

What the player does: collects samples while dust weakens the panels, and uses dust devils to clean them.

Expected learning: something that looks like a danger, a dust devil, could clean the panels.

Simplified or invented: the maze and the extra rovers; the dust on the panels and the cleaning winds are real.

Log 12 · Sun and Shade · solar and nuclear power

Historical context: Spirit and Opportunity ran on solar panels and stopped without light. Curiosity and Perseverance carry a nuclear generator that turns the heat of decaying plutonium-238 into electricity, so they can work at night, in winter and in the shade. NASA gives Curiosity as about 3 m by 2.1 m and 899 kg, against 1.6 m, 1.5 m and 185 kg for Spirit.

What the player does: moves two rovers, one solar and one nuclear, each passing where the other cannot.

Expected learning: where a rover gets its power, and how large that makes it, shape where it can go.

Simplified or invented: rovers do not jump and two never worked side by side. The rover that really ended its mission stuck in soft soil was Spirit, the light solar one. Curiosity and Perseverance are still active and appear only as the nuclear example.

Log 13 · Pathfinder Bounce · Mars Pathfinder

Historical context: on 4 July 1997 Pathfinder hit the Martian air at about 7,300 m/s. Its heat shield slowed it to 400 m/s, a 12.5 m parachute to about 70 m/s, three rockets fired at 98 m, the tether was cut 21.5 m above the ground, and airbags bounced it at least 15 times. The lander is still in Ares Vallis.

What the player does: acts as mission control and triggers the shield, parachute, rockets, airbags and cord cut at the right moments.

Expected learning: because Mars’s air is thin, this mission needed a heat shield, a parachute, rockets and airbags working together.

Simplified or invented: the clock, the falling physics and the limits (parachute tear 600 m/s, airbag 26 m/s). In 1997 the computer, not a person, triggered every step.

Log 14 · Sojourner’s Plan · Sojourner rover

Historical context: Sojourner, the first rover on Mars (1997), was driven from Earth, but radio took 10 to 15 minutes, so it carried hazard avoidance. All its messages went through the lander. Its APXS, which measures what rocks are made of, was at the back. Barnacle Bill was its first rock and Yogi the second.

What the player does: plans a list of moves, sends it and watches it run without being able to correct it.

Expected learning: with minutes of delay, moves are planned ahead and the robot must stop by itself in front of hazards.

Simplified or invented: the grid, the limit of 12 commands per plan and the hidden rocks on level 3.

Log 15 · Phoenix Ice Dig · Phoenix lander

Historical context: Phoenix landed in the Martian arctic on 25 May 2008 and dug 12 trenches. Three bright clumps vanished in four days: ice turning straight into gas. Its first oven sample showed no water, most likely because it had sat in the open. As summer ended heaters were switched off, and the last signal came on 2 November 2008.

What the player does: digs, watches the chunks change over days, labels ice and salt, then tests fresh samples before winter.

Expected learning: watching how something changes over time helps identify what it is, and a solar lander lives only as long as the sunlight lasts.

Simplified or invented: the salt chunks that look like ice, the ice depths and the freshness rule.

Log 16 · Ingenuity: Fly in Thin Air · Ingenuity helicopter

Historical context: the 1.8 kg helicopter made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet on 19 April 2021, in air less than 1% as dense as Earth’s, with blades spinning up to 2,537 rpm. It flew 72 times; on 18 January 2024 a rotor blade was damaged at landing, over steep, featureless sand ripples that gave its navigation camera too little texture. It still stands on Mars.

What the player does: sets the rotor speed to lift off, hover and land, and avoids featureless sand.

Expected learning: in thin air blades must spin very fast to produce lift; the battery limits each flight; the navigation camera needs textured ground.

Simplified or invented: a simplified lift model and a faster spin-up.

EARTH AND ASTEROIDS

Log 17 · Keep the Link · Deep Space Network (still active)

Historical context: to talk to a far probe, an antenna must have it above its horizon, and the Earth turns once a day. NASA’s Deep Space Network has three sites, Goldstone (California), Madrid (Spain) and Canberra (Australia), placed around the world so that at least one can see a probe in most directions.

What the player does: places antennas, runs a whole day and sees when the probe is lost.

Expected learning: because the Earth turns, a single antenna loses the probe for long stretches of each day, and antennas spread around the world cover the day.

Simplified or invented: a fixed probe direction and a simplified 80 degree view from each antenna.

Log 18 · DART Impact · the DART spacecraft

Historical context: on 26 September 2022 NASA flew the 570 kg DART spacecraft into the moonlet Dimorphos at about 22,500 km/h. It slowed the moonlet by a few millimetres per second, shortening its orbit from 11 h 55 min to 11 h 23 min, a difference of 32 minutes. The debris thrown off pushed back and, in NASA’s words, “substantially enhanced DART’s push”.

What the player does: aims the impactor to cut the orbit by a target number of minutes; the last level gives one shot.

Expected learning: a small, fast impact can change an asteroid’s speed; to shorten the moonlet’s orbit the impact must push against its motion, while a push from behind would speed it up and enlarge the orbit; the debris adds to the push.

Simplified or invented: the timing is theatre, and levels 1 and 2 give spare impactors; the real mission had exactly one.
